content: The most severe complications of cystic fibrosis (CF) are related to respiratory insufficiency. Oxygen supplementation therapy has been a long-standing standard treatment for individuals with chronic lung diseases that are associated with hypoxemia. Physicians often prescribe oxygen therapy for patients with CF when hypoxemia is present. However, there is uncertainty regarding whether sufficient empirical evidence exists to justify the use of this therapy, given its financial costs and significant impact on patients' lifestyles. The objective of this review was to determine whether oxygen therapy improves either the longevity or the quality of life of individuals with CF. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, which includes references identified through extensive electronic database searches and manual searches of relevant journals and conference proceedings. The most recent search of the Group's Trials Register was conducted on May 15, 2013. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared oxygen therapy, administered at any concentration and by any route, in individuals with documented CF over any time period. The authors independently assessed the risk of bias in the included studies and extracted relevant data. A total of 11 published studies involving 172 participants were included in the review. Of these, only one study, which involved 28 participants, examined the effects of long-term oxygen therapy. This study found no statistically significant improvements in survival, lung function, or cardiac health. However, individuals receiving oxygen therapy showed improved regular attendance at school or work at both 6 and 12 months. Four studies investigated the effects of oxygen supplementation during sleep using polysomnography. While oxygenation improved, mild hypercapnia (elevated carbon dioxide levels in the blood) was observed. Participants receiving oxygen therapy fell asleep more quickly and spent a smaller percentage of their total sleep time in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. However, there were no measurable improvements in qualitative sleep parameters. Six studies evaluated the effects of oxygen supplementation during exercise. Oxygenation improved in these cases as well, but mild hypercapnia was again noted. Participants receiving oxygen therapy were able to exercise for significantly longer durations. However, other exercise-related parameters were not affected by the use of oxygen therapy. The authors concluded that there is no published evidence to guide the prescription of chronic oxygen supplementation for individuals with advanced lung disease due to CF. While short-term oxygen therapy during sleep and exercise improves oxygenation, it is associated with mild hypercapnia, which is likely to be clinically insignificant. Benefits were observed in terms of increased exercise duration, reduced time to fall asleep, and improved regular attendance at school or work. However, there is a need for larger, well-designed clinical trials to evaluate the potential benefits of long-term oxygen therapy in individuals with CF, whether administered continuously or during specific activities such as exercise or sleep. Unfortunately, the authors do not anticipate any new research in this area in the near future and do not plan to update this review unless new evidence becomes available.
